Dropcho, MD ~___ Paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis developed as the presenting feature of small-cell lung carcinoma in 3 patients. Two patients with paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis manifested predominantly as subacute sensory neuronopathy did not improve after prednisone treatment and chemotherapy. The third patient had seyere axial and limb rigidity and myoclo- nus, which partially improved after chemotherapy and treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin and prednisone. Serum fiom each patient immunocytochemically stained the neuropil and to a lesser degree the neuronal cytoplasm in human cerebral and cerebellar cortex. On immunoblots of human neuronal extracts, each patient’s serum contained high-titer IgG antibodies reacting with a protein band of apparent molecular mass 125 kd. This autoantibody pattern is indistinguishable from antibodies recently identified in several women with breast carcinoma and stiff-man syndrome. Screening of a human brain complementary DNA expression library with patient serum yielded clones whose sequence is identical to that of the synaptic vesicle-related protein amphiphysin. Reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction demonstrated expression of amphiphysin in 8 of 10 small-cell lung carcinomas and in 5 of 14 breast carcinomas. These observations highlight the clinical and serological heterogeneity of paraneoplastic central nervous system disorders: Patients with a given clinical syndrome may have different antineuronal antibodies, and patients with a given autoanti- body specificity have differing clinical presentations. Dropcho EJ. Antiamphiphysin antibodies with small-cell lung carcinoma and paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis. Ann Neurol 1996;39:659-667 Paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis (PEM) encompasses patients with heterogeneous clinical features, tumor as- sociations, and antineuronal autoantibody specificities [l, 21. PEM occurs most frequently in association with small-cell lung carcinoma (SCLC); most of these pa- tients have a prominent sensory neuronopathy and high-titer circulating type I antinuclear antineuronal antibodies (ANNA-I, also called anti-Hu antibodies) that are directed against a number of closely related RNA-binding proteins. A more recently described paraneoplastic disorder features women with breast car- cinoma, “stiff-man syndrome,” and circulating anti- bodies against a protein homologous to the avian syn- aptic vesicle-related protein amphiphysin [3, 41. The 3 patients described here all had SCLC, PEM, and anti- bodies against human amphiphysin, though only I pa- tient had clinical rigidity. Patient Histories Patient 1 In November 1992, a 54-year-old woman experienced numbness and an unpleasant “gritty” sensation of the right hand. Over several months the sensory symptoms spread to involve all four limbs and the face, and she developed pro- gressively unsteady gait, intermittent horizontal diplopia, dysphagia, and right arm weakness. Examination in June 1993 showed a partial right sixth nerve palsy and mild right central facial weakness. There was moderate atrophy of the intrinsic hand muscles, worse on the right side. Strength was 4+/5 except for 3+/5 in the intrinsic hand muscles. She was totally areflexic. She had a moderate, roughly symrnetri- cal decrease in a vibratory sense from the elbows distally

and from the knees distally. Proprioception was markedly diminished in the right hand and to a lesser degree in the left hand and both feet. She was unable to localize either hand in space. There was sensory ataxia of all limbs, worse on the right side. Romberg’s test was positive and gait was wide based and very unsteady; she was barely able to walk even with assistance. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed 9 mononuclear white blood cells (WBCs) /PI, protein concentration of 104 mg/dl, IgG index of 0.9 (normal < 0.7), IgG level of 12.3 mg/dl (normal < 3.8), IgG synthesis rate of 28.8 mg/day (normal < 0), and 2 oligoclonal IgG bands. Eleitromy- ography (EMG) showed fibrillations and positive sharp waves in intrinsic hand muscles. Serum and CSF were found to contain antineurorial antibodies (see below). Biopsy of a paratracheal lymph node revealed SCLC. The patient received a course of intravenous IgG (0.4 gml kglday for 5 days) and was begun on prednisone, 80 ingi day. She received six courses of cisplatin plus etoposide and attained complete remission of the SCLC. After 1 month, prednisone was tapered and discontinued without any change in her symptoms. A second course of intravenous IgG in February 1994 produced transient subjective im- provement in sensory symptoms but no discernible change in her strength or gait. As of January 1995 she was neurologi- cally stable, with persistent numbness and dysesthesias of the face and limbs, weakness mainly involving the hands, and inability to walk due to profound proprioceptive loss and severe retropulsion. Patient 2 In April 1993, a 60-year-old woman experienced mild diffuse weakness, and numbness and dysesthesias in all limbs. On examination in July 1993 strength was 4 to 4+/5 diffusely with somewhat worse weakness in the proximal arm and leg muscles. Proprioception was moderately diminished in the toes and the fingers of the right hand. She had a hyyerpathic response to light touch and pinprick over all four limbs and the trunk. Tendon reflexes were trace in the upper extremi- ties and absent in the lower extremities. Gait was wide based. CSF analysis revealed 27 mononuclear WBCs/pI, protein concentration of 142 mgldl, IgG index of 0.7, IgG level of 27.2 mg/dl, IgG synthesis rate of 49.9 tng/day, and 4 IgG oligoclonal bands. Electrophysiological studies showed absent sensory potentials or reduced compound nerve action poten- tials in several sensory nerves. Antineuronal antibodies were demonstrated in serum and CSF. Biopsy of a large mediasti- nal mass showed SCLC. The patient was begun on prednisone, 80 mg/day, and received two cycles of cisplatin plus etoposide, with partial tumor response. However, her diffuse weakness progressively worsened, as did the numbness and painful dysesthesias of the trunk and limbs. In late August 1993 she additionally trophysiological studies indicated a moderately severe axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy, with denervation in the upper and lower extremities. A sural nerve biopsy specimen showed a mild reduction in the number of myelinated fibers with no inflammation or vasculitis. CSF analysis revealed a protein concentration of 80 mgidl, 30 mononuclear WBCslpl, and a normal IgG index. The stiffness and myoclonus were par- tially ameliorated by combinations of oral valproate, diaze- pam, and baclofen. Over the next 6 weeks the patient’s my- oclonus and rigidity worsened and spread proximally to involve the abdominal and thoracic muscles including the diaphragm, to the point where respiratory difficulty devel- oped. He was maintained on pancuronium, ventilatory sup- port, and heavy sedation for nearly 2 weeks. Biopsy of a subcarinal mass showed SCLC. The patient received a course of intravenous IgG, was be- gun on prednisone, and began monthly chemotherapy with cisplatin plus etoposide. Over the next month his mental

status returned to near baseline and the myoclonus gradually resolved. Serum drawn in September showed antineuronal antibodies (see below). He received a total of six cycles of chemotherapy; after the first two cycles there was a complete remission of the tumor. As of November 1994 he remained unable to walk because of severe, fixed flexion rigidity of both legs. Numbness and dysesthesias of the legs persisted and mild weakness and hyperreflexia of the left arm devel- oped. Materials and Methods Tissue Specimens For extraction of proteins or RNA, normal adult human brain or other tissue obtained at autopsy, human tumors obtained at surgery, or normal adult rodent brains were promptly frozen at -70°C. Frozen tumor specimens were obtained from 10 patients with SCLC (not the present pa- tients), including 7 patients without neurological dysfunc- tion, 2 patients with PEM and high-titer ANNA-I, and 1 patient with “antibody-negative’’ PEM. Tumor specimens were also obtained from 20 women with breast carcinoma and without neurological dysfunction. All human tissues were acquired and handled in accordance with requirements of the Institutional Review Board. - developed severe dysphagia for solids and liquids, constipa- tion, and orthostatic hypotension. Examination in Septem- ber showed absent gag reflex, 3 + / 5 strength diffusely, pro- found loss of proprioception in all limbs, and painful dysesthesias induced by light touch or by a tuning fork. She was unable to stand. She received a course of intravenous methylprednisolone (60 mglday) and intravenous IgG (0.4 gm/kg/day X 5 days), with only minor subjective improve- ment in her strength and swallowing. She elected to discon- time chemotherapy and died 1 month later. Brain tissue frozen in OCT Com- pound was sectioned at 8 pm, fixed in cold acetone, washed with 0.3% hydrogen peroxide (H202) in methanol, and then with 10% normal goat serum in phosphate-buffered saline v .- solution (PBS). Paraffin-embedded brain or tumor tissue was sectioned at 5 pm, and slides were baked at 56°C for 1 hour. Sections were deparaffinized in successive washes with xylene and a graded series of ethanol solutions, washed with 0.5% H,O, in methanol, and then washed with 10% normal goat serum in PBS. Soluble extracts of brain or tumor tissue were prepared by homogenizing the tissue in lysis buffer con- taining Tris-buffered saline, 1% Nonidet P-40 (Sigma, St. Louis, MO), 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, and 0.1% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), followed by incubation at 37°C for 30 minutes, and centrifugation. Neuronal or tissue extracts were resuspended in Laemmli electrophoresis sample buffer [7] containing 2% SDS and 5% 2-mercaptoethanol, boiled for 5 minutes, electropho- resed in 7.5% or 9.0% polyacrylamide gels with 40/0 stack- ings gels, and electrophoretically transferred to nitrocellulose 181. Molecular Cloning Serum from Patient 1 (1 : 500 dilution) was used as an anti- body probe to screen a human hippocampus complementary DNA (cDNA) library (lambda ZAP 11, Stratagene, La Jolla, CA) according to previously published methods [9]. Immu- nosuppressive plaques were identified with affinity-purified goat anti-human IgG by the same technique used in immu- noblots. Results Immunocytochemical Studies Serum from each patient diffusely stained the neuropil of human and rodent frontal cortex, hippocampus, cer- ebellum, and spinal cord in frozen or paraffin-embed- ded sections (Fig 1). There was fairly intense, diffuse staining of the cytoplasm of large hippocampal neu- rons, and less intense staining of Purkinje cell cyto- plasm. In some cerebellar sections the staining of Pur- kinje cells was concentrated at the periphery of the perikarya, suggesting reactivity with synaptic terminals. No other neuronal cell bodies in the brain were stained. Formalin or paraformaldehyde fixation and treatment of deparaffinized sections with lead thiocya- nate yielded the optimal preservation of architecture and intensity of neuropil and neuronal staining. This staining pattern was not produced by normal human serum control samples run simultaneously, nor by more than 400 sera taken from patients with a variety of neurological disorders (including other paraneoplas- tic disorders) studied in this laboratory. Serum from Patient 2 additionally stained the nuclei and cytoplasm of all neurons in frozen brain sections in a pattern typical of ANNA-1 [14]. The ANNA-1 staining pattern was absent in tissue that had under- gone paraformaldehyde or overnight formalin fixation. Neu ronal Im m u no blotting Serum from each patient reacted with a broad band of apparent molecular mass 125 kd in immunoblots of isolated human cortical neurons and of Purkinje cells (Fig 2). The band was also abundantly present in solu- ble lysates of human cerebral and cerebellar cortex. In some experiments two or three closely spaced bands were seen rather than a single broad band. In human cortical neuronal immunoblots this reactivity was pres- ent up to end point serum dilutions of 1 : IOO,OOO,OOO, 1 : 20,000,000, and 1 : 50,000,000 in the 3 patients. No reactivity was seen when affinity-purified anti-human IgM was used as the secondary antibody. The electro- phoretic mobility of the band(s) did not differ in the presence or absence of 2-mercaptoethanol in the sam- ple buffer, or whether the lysates were boiled prior to loading onto the gel. A band of nearly identical size was present in blots of lysates of cerebral or cerebellar cortex from mice and rats, and of rat thoracic spinal cord. A second, fainter band of apparent molecular mass 112 kd was present in immunoblots of rat cere- bellum. CSF from Patients 1 and 2 obtained at the same time as their initial serum sample showed the same pattern of reactivity as serum. An “antineuronal anti- body index” was calculated as follows, using the recip- rocals of end point titers from neuronal immunoblots:

(CSF antibody titer/serum antibody titer)/(CSF IgG/ serum IgG). This index was 3.1 for Patient 1 and 1.1 for Patient 2; an index above 1.0 suggests selective in- trathecal synthesis or retention of antineuronal anti- bodies. Serum from Patient 2 additionally showed antibody reactivity with a group of 35- to 40-kd neuronal pro- teins identical to an ANNA-1 pattern, at an end point dilution of 1 : 200,000 in neuronal immunoblots. ANNA-1 reactivity was confirmed by high-titer serum reactivity with the Hel-N1 autoantigen in an enzyme- linked immunoassay [ 151. Serial serum samples were available from each pa- tient. The high serum antineuronal antibody titer in Patient 1 did not fall after her treatment with predni- sone, intravenous IgG, and initial cycles of chemother- apy. From January through June 1994 the serum titer fell approximately 20-fold, in the setting of stable neurological dysfunction. In Patient 2, the titers of ANNA-1 and the novel antineuronal antibodies both fell fourfold in the month following treatment with prednisone and intravenous IgG, and initiation of che- motherapy. During that time the patient’s neurological condition markedly worsened. Patient 3’s antineuronal antibody titer fell 40-fold from the baseline, pretreat- ment sample in December 1993 to November 1994, at which time he remained in complete remission from SCLC and had made a partial neurological recovery. Reactivity with the 125-kd autoantigen was not de- tected in human neuronal immunoblots with sera from any of 46 patients with SCLC, 16 of whom had PEM and high-titer ANNA-I. Molecular Cloning Antibody screening of 250,000 phage plaques from a human hippocampus lambda ZAP I1 cDNA library by serum from Patient 1 yielded four reproducibly posi- tive cDNA clones, designated bol to bo4 (Fig 3). The consensus nucleotide sequence of the clones (see Fig 3) features an open reading frame of 1,065 bp that is identical to the nucleotide sequence of human amphi- physin reported by David and colleagues [16] (Gen- Bank accession number U076 16). Discussion In 1993 Folli and coauthors [4] reported on 3 women in whom stiff-man syndrome was the presenting fea- ture of breast carcinoma. Each patient had circulating autoantibodies that stained the neuropil of rat brain, and reacted with a protein doublet of approximately 128 kd in immunoblots of human cerebral cortex. Two additional women with breast carcinoma, stiff-man syndrome, and similar autoantibodies have since been reported [3, 161, although detailed clinical descriptions were not provided. Grimaldi and colleagues [ 171 men- tioned autoantibodies against a 125- to 130-kd protein associated with stiff-man syndrome in 1 patient with colon carcinoma and 1 with Hodgkin’s disease; no fur- ther details on the characteristics of these antibodies were provided. De Camilli and associates [3] showed that the 128- kd brain protein reacting with serum from patients with breast carcinoma and stiff-man syndrome had the same electrophoretic mobility as a protein reacting with affinity-purified antibodies raised against chicken am- phiphysin. Their patients’ sera also reacted with a re- combinant chicken amphiphysin fusion protein. David and coworkers [16] subsequently used probes derived from the chicken amphiphysin gene to clone its human analogue, and showed that rabbit antisera raised against recombinant human amphiphysin reacted with the 128-kd “stiff-man autoantigen” in rat brain. The presence of antiamphiphysin antibodies in the 3 present patients is supported by the following evi- dence: (1) The immunocytochemical staining pattern produced by patients’ sera is very similar if not identi- cal to that of the breast carcinoma patients of Folli and coauthors [4], and to the pattern produced by rabbit antiserum raised against recombinant chicken amphi- physin [18]. (2) Reactivity of patients’ sera with a pro- tein antigen on immunoblots of human and animal brain is indistinguishable from that of previously re- ported patients with antiamphiphysin antibodies. Par- enthetically, in present studies and previous reports the apparent molecular mass of chicken and human am- phiphysin (125-128 kd) based on electrophoretic mo- bility is considerably greater than the mass (75.2 kd and 76.2 kd, respectively) based on the nucleotide se- quence 1181. (3) The present cDNA clones encoding amphiphysin were isolated by virtue of their reactivity with Patient 1’s circulating antibodies. (4) Each pa- tient’s serum reacted with recombinant amphiphysin proteins, and preabsorption of the sera with recombi- nant bol protein diminished reactivity with the 125- kd human neuronal antigen. The specific role of amphiphysin in synaptic trans- mission is not yet known [19, 201. The pattern and widespread distribution of antiamphiphysin immuno- reactivity closely resembles that of synaptophysin [4, 181. Chicken amphiphysin is abundant in synapto- soma1 preparations and in presynaptic terminals by electron microscopy, but is also present in the neuronal

cytosol [18]. Both the avian and human forms of am- phiphysin are hydrophilic, and neither features a hy- drophobic domain that would indicate an integral syn- aptic vesicle membrane location [ 16, 181. Amphiphysin contains putative phosphorylation sites for several pro- tein kinases, and also contains a proline-rich domain that may enable it to bind to “src homology 3” (SH3) domains of proteins involved in intracellular signal transduction [ 16, 211. In an effort to identify immunodominant epitope(s) reacting with antiamphiphysin antibodies, David and coauthors [16] reported reactivity of sera from 5 pa- tients with breast cancer with the C-terminal 150- amino acid fragment of human amphiphysin. They ob- served less intense and more variable immunoreactivity of patients’ sera with other portions of the protein. Sera from each of the 3 SCLC patients in the present study reacted strongly with recombinant proteins encoded by three cDNA clones that share the 208 C-terminal amino acids of amphiphysin. Preabsorption with the bol fusion protein did not completely abolish patients’ serum reactivity with amphiphysin in neuronal immu- noblots. This suggests that a portion of the autoanti- body response is directed against epitope(s) on the N- terminal end of amphiphysin, or that epitope(s) created by posttranslational modification or secondary struc- ture of amphiphysin are not present on recombinant segments of the protein. The present patients expand the spectrum of clinical features and tumor types associated with antiamphiphy- sin antibodies. There are several reports of patients with SCLC and PEM who had rigidity and spasms believed to be caused by damage or loss of spinal cord interneurons [22,23]. These patients were not tested for antineuronal antibodies. Muscle rigidity resembling stiff-man syn- drome has been observed in several patients with a variety of other neoplasms, including thymoma [24,25], Hodg- kin’s disease [ 171, and carcinomas of the breast or colon [ 171. Two patients with thymoma and paraneoplastic ri- gidity reported by Nicholas and associates [25] did not have identifiable antineuronal antibodies. Rigidity in the present patients with SCLC and antiamphiphysin anti- bodies and in the previously reported patients with breast carcinoma presumably reflects pathology in the spinal cord or brainstem or both, although direct pathological proof is lacking. Antiamphiphysin antibodies are not restricted to pa- tients with stiff-man syndrome. Two of the present pa- tients had prominent dysesthesias that began asymmet- rically and involved the face, trunk, and proximal limbs early in the course, and also had areflexia, dispropor- tionate loss of proprioception, and loss of sensory nerve action potentials. These features are typical of para- neoplastic sensory neuronopathy caused by injury to dorsal root ganglia neurons [26, 271. The pattern and severity of sensory dysfunction in Patient 1 did not differ from those of patients with sensory neuronopa- thy and ANNA-I whom I personally examined. Except for the additional presence of ANNA-1 in Patient 2, the patterns of antiamphiphysin immunore- activity by immunocytochemistry and immunoblotting were indistinguishable among the present 3 patients, despite their differing clinical presentations. Diffuse reactivity of antiamphiphysin antibodies throughout the central nervous system (CNS) is reminiscent of the panneuronal reactivity of ANNA-1 and ANNA-2 (anti-Ri antibodies) [l]. For each of these three para- neoplastic autoantibodies there is a predominant clini- cal syndrome (stiff-man syndrome, sensory neuronopa- thy, and opsoclonus/ataxia, respectively), but patients with a given autoantibody are clinically heterogeneous. To date, individual patient’s clinical features do not correlate with identifiably different patterns of immu- noreactivity of their sera with specific neuronal subsets. As with several other antineuronal autoantibodies, antiamphiphysin antibodies appear to be a useful tool for diagnosing a patient’s neurological disorder as para- neoplastic, and for indicating the probable type of underlying neoplasm [I]. The actual role of antiam- phiphysin antibodies in the pathogenesis of PEM or stiff-man syndrome is unknown. The general theory of autoimmunity for neurological paraneoplastic syn- dromes is that the immune response initially arises as an antitumor response directed against shared anti- gen(s) expressed by tumor cells and neurons [l]. Folli and colleagues [4] did not detect amphiphysin in im- munoblots of the breast tumor from one of their para- neoplastic stiff-man patients, nor from 12 breast carci- nomas from neurologically normal patients. In the present study expression of amphiphysin was more eas- ily detected by RT-PCR than by immunoblotting. It is not known whether this is due to the greater sensitiv-

ity of RT-PCR or to differences in immunoreactivity of amphiphysin expressed by neurons versus tumor cells. The RT-PCR results also suggest the possibility of alternate splicing of amphiphysin RNA in tumors; this is presently under further study. Expression of the amphiphysin gene in some SCLCs and breast carcino- mas indirectly supports the general theory of auto- immunity in paraneoplastic disorders, but does not provide insight into the mechanism(s) of immune- mediated neuronal injury. Three of the 5 reported patients with breast cancer, stiff-man syndrome, and antiamphiphysin antibodies had neurological improvement with prednisone and tu- mor resection [4, 161. Of the 3 patients reported in detail by Folli and colleagues [4], one became “neuro- logically normal” and one regained independent ambu- lation. The third patient was not treated with steroids and had progressive rigidity despite treatment by tumor resection, diazepam, and baclofen [4]. Patient 3 in the present report partially improved with chemotherapy and immunotherapy, but still could not walk. The other 2 present patients did not improve despite che- motherapy, corticosteroids, and intravenous immuno- globulin (and a fall in antiamphiphysin antibody ti- ters). Their clinical course was more typical of PEM and SCLC [I, 21, namely, either a pattern of subacute deterioration and subsequent leveling off at severe neu- rological disability (Patient I), or progressive neurolog- ical deterioration despite aggressive treatment (Patient 2). The small number of reported patients with anti- amphiphysin antibodies does not allow any firm state- ments as to whether patients with breast carcinoma have a better neurological outcome than do patients with SCLC. Until more data become available, it seems reasonable to treat patients with paraneoplastic disor- ders and antiamphiphysin antibodies with a combina- tion of antitumor treatment, corticosteroids, and possi- bly intravenous immunoglobulin.
